vignette:
James Kofi's Careful Calculations

James Kofi sits in the therapy office with his laptop closed beside him-a habit born of decades in software engineering, always keeping work within arm's reach. At seventy-seven, he carries himself with the precision of someone accustomed to solving problems methodically, yet his hands occasionally tremble as he speaks about the 1990s.

He came to the United States in 1992, fleeing ethnic violence in his home country. He was thirty-nine then, a mathematics teacher with two young children and a wife who trusted him to get them to safety. The journey itself-the nights hidden in strangers' homes, the border crossing, the refugee camp where they spent fourteen months-these details emerge slowly, as though James must first calculate whether it is safe to speak them aloud.

What he remembers most vividly is the waiting. Not the danger itself, but the endless, suffocating uncertainty. In the camp, he would wake at 3 a.m., his heart racing, convinced that soldiers had come. His wife would find him standing at the tent opening, watching darkness that held no visible threat. His children learned not to cry at night.

When they finally arrived in America, James threw himself into rebuilding with characteristic discipline. He taught himself programming through library books and night courses, eventually becoming a software engineer at a mid-sized tech firm. He was good at it-the logic, the problem-solving, the way code followed rules that made sense. For many years, he felt almost normal. He built a life: a house in the suburbs, a stable job, his children graduated and thriving.

But the mind, he has learned, keeps its own calendar.

About five years ago, after he retired, something shifted. Without the structure of work-the meetings, the deadlines, the constant mental engagement-the waiting returned. Now he finds himself unable to sleep more than four hours a night, his mind cycling through scenarios he cannot control. He lies beside his wife, careful not to wake her, running through calculations that have no solution: What if they hadn't left? What if the camp had closed? What if the paperwork had been rejected?

He startles easily. Last month, his grandson knocked on the door unexpectedly, and James found himself on the floor before he realized what had happened. His wife helped him up without comment, but he saw the worry in her eyes.

The hypervigilance manifests in ways both obvious and subtle. He monitors the news obsessively, tracking global conflicts with the intensity he once brought to debugging code. He maintains detailed spreadsheets of their finances and documents, though they are secure. When his wife mentions traveling to visit family, his stomach tightens immediately-the thought of borders, of documents, of being trapped somewhere unfamiliar triggers a cascade of physical responses he cannot simply think away.

He avoids certain neighborhoods that remind him of the camp's layout. He cannot watch films depicting violence or displacement. Crowds make him anxious; he calculates exits before entering any space. His daughter suggested therapy years ago, but he resisted-a man who survived, who built a successful life, should not need help. Yet here he is, finally, because his wife gently insisted, and because even his considerable discipline cannot quiet the part of him that remains thirty-nine years old, waiting in darkness, trying to protect people he loves from a threat he cannot see.
